classification.difficultyReason: Recall bearing conventions and distinguish an acute-angle interval from one including cardinal-direction endpoints.

questions.mappingNote: Printed items 1–3 test the true-bearing definition and leading-zero convention; item 4 tests the compass-bearing starting direction; item 5 tests the source's intended exclusion of cardinal-direction endpoints.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 defines true bearings clockwise from North using three digits, and compass bearings as acute angles from North or South towards East or West. Pages 2–4 supply the preceding right-triangle and elevation/depression teaching context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognises the definitions and notation conventions for true and compass bearings.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguishes the observation point and direction in reciprocal bearing statements.

questions.mappingNote: The question assesses the location of the bearing's reference point and the direction of observation, rather than calculating an angle.
questions.methodNote: Figure 31 on page 5 places the North reference at B for A from B, and at A for B from A.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguishes the observation point and direction in reciprocal bearing statements.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalises reciprocal true bearings and handles both angle ranges to keep the result within one revolution.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 generalises the reciprocal-bearing relationship illustrated by Figure 31; it assesses bearing interpretation and angular wraparound.
questions.methodNote: Figure 31 gives reciprocal true bearings of 065° and 245°. Reverse the direction by 180° and keep the result in the true-bearing range.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalises reciprocal true bearings and handles both angle ranges to keep the result within one revolution.

classification.difficultyReason: Identifies the angle measured below the horizontal at the upper observation point.

questions.mappingNote: The upper dashed horizontal in question 8 identifies the reference line. Its sector with the descending diagonal is α; β uses the vertical reference instead.
questions.methodNote: PDF page 4 defines depression as the angle below the horizontal and contrasts correct horizontal measurement with incorrect vertical measurement in the cliff example.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identifies the angle measured below the horizontal at the upper observation point.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify sides relative to the marked angle, select a trigonometric ratio, and rearrange it when the unknown is the denominator.

questions.mappingNote: All six assigned items share one side-finding instruction. Questions 12–15 require rearranging a ratio containing x in the denominator; each child's mapping identifies its actual side placement.
questions.methodNote: Use the printed sine, cosine and tangent definitions and the length-finding example: identify the relevant sides, substitute, rearrange and round only the final length.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select and rearrange right-triangle ratios, including cases where the unknown length is in the denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the two supplied sides, select the matching ratio, and apply its inverse to find the marked angle.

questions.mappingNote: All three printed items assess an unknown acute angle in a right-angled triangle. Page 2 supplies the ratio definitions and page 3 supplies the inverse-ratio method.
questions.methodNote: Select the trigonometric ratio using the given sides, apply its inverse in degree mode and round to the requested precision.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the ratio from two given sides and apply an inverse trigonometric function.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the true bearing into an angle south of east, form a right triangle, and select sine for the southerly component.

questions.mappingNote: Page 5 establishes clockwise true bearings; page 2 demonstrates finding an opposite length using sine. The assessed result is a directional distance component.
questions.methodNote: Interpret the clockwise bearing from north, form a right triangle and use sine to calculate the opposite component from the hypotenuse.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret a true bearing and resolve the journey into its southerly component.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret 200 degrees as west of south and use the resulting right triangle to isolate the westerly distance.

questions.mappingNote: Page 5 supplies the true-bearing convention; page 2 supplies the right-triangle sine method. The question combines bearing interpretation with finding a distance.
questions.methodNote: Interpret the true bearing as 20 degrees west of south and use sine to calculate the opposite component from the hypotenuse.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert the bearing into a triangle angle and calculate the westerly component.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent the compass direction as a right triangle and identify the easterly component as opposite the given angle.

questions.mappingNote: Page 5 defines compass bearings and illustrates north-to-east measurement; page 2 demonstrates the sine method for an unknown opposite length.
questions.methodNote: Measure the compass-bearing angle from north towards east and use sine to calculate the opposite component.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read the compass bearing and use trigonometry to find the easterly component.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent the north-west direction and choose cosine because the requested northerly component is adjacent to the bearing angle.

questions.mappingNote: Page 5 defines compass bearings from north towards west; page 2 defines cosine as adjacent divided by hypotenuse. A practical directional distance component is assessed.
questions.methodNote: Interpret N50 degrees W, identify the northerly component as adjacent to the given angle and use cosine.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read the compass bearing and identify the northerly component as adjacent to the given angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that exchanging the observation points reverses the direction and subtract 180 degrees.

questions.mappingNote: Question 23 reverses the fisherman-to-whale direction; subtract 180° because the given bearing exceeds 180°.
questions.methodNote: Measure true bearings clockwise from north at the from-point. Reciprocal bearings differ by 180°.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reverse the direction between two points by changing the true bearing by 180°.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse the campsite-to-landmark direction by adding 180 degrees to the given bearing.

questions.mappingNote: Question 24 exchanges the campsite and landmark as the from-point and destination; add 180° to 075°.
questions.methodNote: Reciprocal true bearings differ by 180° and use three-digit notation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the reciprocal true bearing.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert successive perpendicular journeys into a displacement triangle, use inverse tangent, adjust to a clockwise true bearing, and reverse it.

questions.mappingNote: Question 25(a) uses the 5 km east and 10 km south components to find the home-to-school bearing. Part (b) applies the reciprocal-bearing rule to the same displacement.
questions.methodNote: Use opposite and adjacent displacement components in the tangent ratio, find the acute angle with inverse tangent, then measure true bearings clockwise from north.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct the displacement triangle, find an acute angle and convert it to forward and reciprocal bearings.

classification.difficultyReason: Build the south-west displacement triangle, calculate its direction with inverse tangent, convert to true bearing, and obtain the reciprocal bearing.

questions.mappingNote: Question 26(a) uses the 12 km west and 4 km south components to find Jane’s bearing from the campsite. Part (b) reverses that direction and requires a leading zero.
questions.methodNote: Use inverse tangent on perpendicular displacement components, then express the direction as a clockwise true bearing. Reverse bearings differ by 180°.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use perpendicular journey components to find a bearing and its reciprocal.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify height and horizontal distance as the tangent sides and use the supplied ratio directly without calculating the angle.

questions.mappingNote: The given tangent ratio and 48 m horizontal distance determine the height directly; calculating the angle is unnecessary.
questions.methodNote: Use tangent as opposite height divided by adjacent horizontal distance, following the ratio definitions and the elevation example.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the given tangent ratio directly with the horizontal distance.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret depression relative to the horizontal, obtain horizontal travel using tangent, and connect that distance to speed over five seconds.

questions.mappingNote: The 200 m vertical height and 5 degree depression angle determine horizontal travel over the stated five seconds.
questions.methodNote: Measure depression from the horizontal, identify the equal elevation angle, and rearrange tangent to find the horizontal distance, following the cliff example. Then use speed equals distance divided by time.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find horizontal displacement from an angle of depression, then divide by elapsed time to determine speed.

classification.difficultyReason: Introduce an unknown ground distance, link two elevation triangles through their shared height and 20-metre separation, and eliminate a variable using exact ratios.

questions.mappingNote: Both observations share the tower height; the difference of their horizontal distances determines that height in exact form.
questions.methodNote: Use tangent in each elevation triangle and the exact values tan 30 degrees equals 1 over square root 3 and tan 60 degrees equals square root 3. Relate the horizontal distances through the stated 20 m approach.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Relate two elevation triangles with a common height and a 20 m change in horizontal distance, using exact trigonometric values.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the common tower height, calculate it from Mary's triangle, then use it in Bob's triangle to find his distance.

questions.mappingNote: The two elevation triangles share the same vertical height. The approved clarification makes their common horizontal ground explicit.
questions.methodNote: Apply tangent to Mary's elevation triangle to find the height, then rearrange tangent in Bob's triangle for his horizontal distance. Retain the unrounded height until the final calculation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use Mary's elevation triangle to establish the tower height and Bob's elevation triangle to determine his horizontal distance.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret a given ratio as triangle side lengths, recover the missing side with Pythagoras, and form a different exact trigonometric ratio.

questions.mappingNote: Printed 31–33 share one acute-angle instruction and become a, b, c. Each item assesses converting a given side ratio into another ratio, without calculating an angle.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines sine, cosine and tangent as right-triangle side ratios. Page 3 supports exact values and exact triangle lengths. Pages 4–5 concern elevation, depression and bearings and do not change the method for these items.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer a missing right-triangle side from one ratio, then form another ratio. Defining trigonometric ratios is the closest catalogue match.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute standard exact ratios and select suitable fraction and conjugate manipulations to simplify the surd quotients.

questions.mappingNote: Printed 34–42 share one instruction and become a–i in numerical order. Items 34–38 assess sums, squares and differences; 39–40 assess fractions and surds; 41–42 assess products and sums or differences. No angle-addition formula is required.
questions.methodNote: Use the exact-value table and special triangles on page 3. Substitute the individual ratios and simplify with exact arithmetic. The displayed instruction prohibits a calculator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute exact trigonometric ratios and simplify fractions and surds. The catalogue lacks an exact-value simplification skill; calculator evaluation conflicts with the explicit calculator prohibition.

classification.difficultyReason: Supply the centre's angle-bisector property, introduce the useful centre-to-vertex triangle, and compare symbolic lengths from two right triangles.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) uses cosine in triangle OCM; part (b) compares exact heights calculated using tangent and sine. The required equilateral-centre angle-bisector property is not explicitly taught in the supplied teaching pages.
questions.methodNote: Use the right-triangle ratio definitions on page 2 and the exact 30°–60°–90° values and triangle on page 3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine equilateral-triangle centre geometry with exact right-triangle ratios to find a length and a height proportion.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct symbolic side lengths from the sine ratio, simplify a difference of squares, and recognise that a positive side requires an absolute value because a may be negative.

questions.mappingNote: The symbolic task directly extends the taught side-ratio definitions. It requires positive side lengths because the angle is acute; the printed stem does not restrict a to positive values.
questions.methodNote: Interpret sine as opposite over hypotenuse, obtain the adjacent side using Pythagoras, and apply the cosine and tangent definitions from page 2. Substitute the derived ratios in part (b).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive parameterised cosine and tangent ratios from a sine ratio, respecting acute-angle signs, then simplify the squared sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Express two adjacent sides using cosine, then combine their lengths into a symbolic proof.

questions.mappingNote: The perpendicular creates triangles ACP and BCP. Cosine gives their base components x and y; AB is their sum. This follows the answer-book hint rather than introducing a different method.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines cosine as adjacent/hypotenuse and demonstrates rearranging a trigonometric ratio to find a length. Pages 3–5 were inspected as the supplied exercise teaching context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express two adjacent sides using cosine, then combine their lengths into a symbolic proof.

classification.difficultyReason: Prove the angles equal through complementary angles, identify tangent sides in two differently oriented triangles, and equate the scaffolded ratios.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) uses the right angles at Z and T. Part (b) applies tangent in YZT and XZT, retaining a and b as hypotenuse-segment lengths. Part (c) equates those ratios and cross-multiplies, following the teacher's stated sequence.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines tangent as opposite/adjacent. The supplied answer evidence uses complementary angles followed by two tangent ratios and their equality.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Prove an angle equality, identify two tangent ratios and equate them to establish a symbolic length identity. Defining and identifying the ratios is the closest supplied catalogue match.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires angle reasoning, exact right-triangle lengths and a geometric decomposition to establish an exact sine value. Right-triangle problem solving is the closest catalogue match.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) uses the supplied perpendicular and horizontal construction. Part (b) applies exact sine and cosine of 30° in OPQ. Part (c) applies sine of 45° in PXQ and OQR, adds PX and QR to obtain PY, and uses the sine definition in OPY.
questions.methodNote: Use the right-triangle sine and cosine definitions on page 2 and the exact special-angle values on page 3. Deduce the final sine value by adding vertical lengths rather than invoking a compound-angle identity. Pages 4 and 5 were inspected and provide application and bearing context, without an additional method needed here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires angle reasoning, exact right-triangle lengths and a geometric decomposition to establish an exact sine value. Right-triangle problem solving is the closest catalogue match.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect quadrant coordinate signs to cosine and sine, and use the sign of y divided by x for gradient and tangent.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) assess coordinate signs; (c) assesses the gradient sign; (d), (e) and (f) connect those signs to the trigonometric ratios. The catalogue has no separate quadrant-sign skill, so quadrant-form relationships are the closest match.
questions.methodNote: Use the unit-circle definitions: cosine is the x-coordinate, sine is the y-coordinate, and tangent is the gradient y/x. Determine signs from quadrant coordinates.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recall the signs of coordinates and trigonometric ratios in the four quadrants. Quadrant-form relationships are the closest catalogue match.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify each angle's quadrant and calculate its acute related angle.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a), (f) and (g) use the supplementary-angle form; (b) and (d) use the third-quadrant form; (c), (e), (h) and (i) use the fourth-quadrant form. This directly assesses the related-angle component of quadrant-form relationships.
questions.methodNote: The related angle is the acute first-quadrant angle. Write second-quadrant angles as 180 degrees minus theta, third-quadrant angles as 180 degrees plus theta, and fourth-quadrant angles as 360 degrees minus theta.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify each angle's quadrant and calculate its acute related angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish the half-turn and full-turn periodic behaviour of the three ratios.

questions.mappingNote: Printed 3 and 4 test the sign reversal of sine and cosine after a half-turn; 5 tests the unchanged tangent gradient; 6 tests full-turn equivalence. The quadrant-form catalogue skill is the closest match for this shared task.
questions.methodNote: Use coterminal rays, unit-circle coordinates and gradients, and the identities for angles of the form 180° + θ.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguish the half-turn and full-turn periodic behaviour of the three ratios.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise correct symmetry, parity and periodic identities, including comparisons between two transformed angles.

questions.mappingNote: Printed 7–9 test half-turn identities; 10–12 test parity; 13 compares full-turn and half-turn sine values; 14 tests fourth-quadrant cosine; 15 compares fourth- and second-quadrant tangent identities. Quadrant-form identities are the main assessed skill; parity has no separate catalogue entry.
questions.methodNote: Apply supplementary and symmetry identities, full-turn equivalence, and the even/odd properties, interpreting sine and cosine as coordinates and tangent as gradient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise correct symmetry, parity and periodic identities, including comparisons between two transformed angles.

classification.difficultyReason: Read axis-point unit-circle coordinates and recognise that tangent is undefined when the x-coordinate is zero.

questions.mappingNote: 16 and 17 use the coordinates (1,0) at 0 degrees; 18 uses their quotient. 19 and 20 use (0,1) at 90 degrees; 21 has a zero denominator. 22 and 23 use (-1,0) at 180 degrees; 24 uses their quotient. 25 and 26 use (0,-1) at 270 degrees; 27 has a zero denominator.
questions.methodNote: Use unit-circle coordinates: cosine is the x-coordinate, sine is the y-coordinate, and tangent is y/x. Evaluate the four axis points exactly; tangent is undefined when x is zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read sine and cosine from unit-circle axis points and recognise zero or undefined tangent.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply supplementary, symmetry and negative-angle identities. The catalogue has no dedicated odd/even identity skill.

questions.mappingNote: Questions 40–42 correspond to page 11; 43–48 correspond to page 12, with tangent comparisons also on page 11; 49–51 correspond to page 14.
questions.methodNote: Simplify directly using supplementary identities, third- and fourth-quadrant symmetry identities, and the odd/even properties of sine, cosine and tangent. Explain signs through coordinates or ray gradients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply supplementary, symmetry and negative-angle identities. The catalogue has no dedicated odd/even identity skill.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a reference triangle, use Pythagoras and combine quadrant or sign information to obtain another exact ratio.

questions.mappingNote: All six assigned items request another exact ratio from a supplied ratio and interval or sign condition.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 teaches reference-triangle construction using ratio magnitudes, Pythagoras and quadrant selection from ratio signs. Pages 9–12 establish signed coordinates, gradients and quadrant relationships; page 13 demonstrates exact-value notation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a reference triangle, use Pythagoras and combine quadrant or sign information to obtain another exact ratio.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow negative rotations to unit-circle axis points and read the required signed coordinate.

questions.mappingNote: Each item evaluates sine or cosine at a negative quarter-turn multiple; direct coordinate readings follow the taught definitions.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines clockwise angles as negative and sine/cosine as signed unit-circle coordinates. Page 14 supplies negative-angle identities consistent with these coordinate evaluations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read sine and cosine values at negative multiples of 90 degrees using signed unit-circle coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify both equal-ratio angles in a closed degree interval using unit-circle symmetry and equal ray gradients.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve assigned equations directly assess equal coordinates or equal gradients. The exact-value and given-ratio demonstrations on pages 13–14 provide context but are not required solution procedures for this write-down task.
questions.methodNote: Interpret sine and cosine as unit-circle coordinates and tangent as ray gradient. Apply the supplementary and symmetry identities to find every equal-ratio angle in the stated closed degree interval.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify both equal-ratio angles in a closed degree interval using unit-circle symmetry and equal ray gradients.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute negative x throughout composite functions, track factor and quotient signs, and compare the complete result with both f(x) and its negative.

questions.mappingNote: All six printed items share one parity-classification instruction. Page 14 explicitly supplies the required negative-angle identities.
questions.methodNote: Compare each complete function at x and -x using sine's and tangent's odd identities and cosine's even identity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Classify functions by substituting a negative argument and applying the even and odd trigonometric identities. This is the closest supplied catalogue skill; none directly covers function parity.

classification.difficultyReason: Express even and odd integers as full turns with a possible half-turn, then encode the scaffolded sign cases in a single expression using (-1)^n.

questions.mappingNote: Part a removes integer full revolutions; part b removes full revolutions and applies the page 12 identity sin(180° + θ) = −sin θ. Part c encodes these two sign cases with (−1)^n.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 establishes full-turn equivalence; pages 11–12 develop supplementary and symmetry identities through unit-circle coordinates. Page 13 demonstrates their use, and page 14 gives odd/even properties.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explains integer half-turns using parity and combines the two sine identities into one expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine integer half-turn behaviour with odd/even identities for negative angles, keeping track of parity-dependent signs.

questions.mappingNote: 95 uses even/odd half-turns for cosine; 96 uses the page 12 tangent half-turn identity; 97 applies question 94 to −θ and page 14 sine oddness; 98 combines the cosine half-turn result with cosine evenness; 99 combines tangent half-turn equivalence with tangent oddness. The integer meaning of n is inherited from the immediately preceding question 94.
questions.methodNote: Use full-turn equivalence, the supplementary and third-quadrant identities, and the odd/even properties of sine, cosine and tangent. Tangent is interpreted as the gradient of the terminal ray.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalises cosine and tangent quadrant identities to integer half-turns and combines them with odd/even properties.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand the odd multiple of 180 degrees into full revolutions and one half-turn, then apply the appropriate taught identity.

questions.mappingNote: 100 uses sin(180° + θ) = −sin θ; 101 uses cos(180° + θ) = −cos θ; 102 uses tan(180° + θ) = tan θ. Each supplied angle is 360n° + 180° + θ.
questions.methodNote: Remove integer full revolutions, then use the page 12 symmetry identities for 180° + θ, following the substitution-and-identity sequence demonstrated on page 13.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognises an odd number of half-turns and applies the taught third-quadrant identities.

classification.difficultyReason: Introduce a perpendicular projection or use equal gradients to connect the unit-circle radius with the tangent-line triangle, then interpret its unit horizontal run.

questions.mappingNote: Apply similarity between the unit-circle projection triangle and the triangle whose horizontal run reaches the tangent number line. The source brace labels the tangent-line value x. Intentionally rename that variable to t in the editable diagram and authored answers, preserving the horizontal x-axis and the tangent line's fixed horizontal coordinate 1.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 extends the unit-circle radius to the tangent at horizontal coordinate 1 and interprets the signed vertical length as tan theta. Page 9 identifies tan theta with the gradient of the radius. The teacher answer explicitly directs use of similar triangles.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires interpreting a radial projection onto a tangent number line through similar triangles and gradient. Ratio derivation is the closest catalogue match; no special-angle evaluation is assessed.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish usable opposite side-angle data from insufficient givens and judge supplementary candidates using the triangle angle-sum restriction.

questions.mappingNote: Printed items 1–2 assess applicability; items 3–6 assess the occurrence and validity of the ambiguous case.
questions.methodNote: Identify an opposite angle–side pair, apply the sine rule, and test supplementary angle candidates against the givens and triangle angle sum.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires distinguishing sine-rule applicability from the occurrence and validity of supplementary angle candidates.

classification.difficultyReason: Judge candidate validity independently of the drawn shape and recognise that a right angle in one possible configuration need not eliminate a second oblique triangle.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 uses the rejected supplementary candidate on page 22. Question 9 explicitly distinguishes a diagram-suggested obtuse angle from the acute candidate, resolving the source's undefined “original case”. Question 10 explicitly concerns SSA data with one possible right-angled configuration and is checked with two valid configurations, one right-angled and one oblique.
questions.methodNote: Find the acute inverse-sine candidate and its supplement, then require the sum with the given angle to be less than 180°.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Tests candidate validity and whether different angle configurations satisfy the triangle angle sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires explaining the angle-sum step and the use of opposite side–angle pairs to calculate missing sides.

questions.mappingNote: The second length example on page 19 supplies the preliminary angle-sum step; the rule on page 18 supplies the three opposite pairs.
questions.methodNote: Find the third angle when necessary, then use the known opposite side–angle pair to find each unknown length.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires explaining the angle-sum step and the use of opposite side–angle pairs to calculate missing sides.

classification.difficultyReason: State the taught prerequisite that the known angle must be opposite a known side, providing a complete sine-rule pair.

questions.mappingNote: The rule and the opposite-pair reminder on pages 18–19 establish the prerequisite; page 20 illustrates it for SSA data.
questions.methodNote: Identify a complete opposite side–angle pair before applying the sine rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identifies the complete opposite side–angle pair needed to apply the sine rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that the requested angle cannot be found directly, calculate both possible values of B, validate them, and use each to find theta.

questions.mappingNote: Question 25 requires finding angle B first because theta has no labelled opposite side. The ambiguous-angle examples on PDF pages 20–22 establish the candidate and validity checks; page 19 establishes the additional angle-sum step.
questions.methodNote: Use sine-over-opposite-side ratios to find an angle, calculate the supplementary candidate, test the triangle angle sum, and then find the third angle. Preserve the inverse-sine function's single principal output.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find both possible values of an intermediate angle, test them, then find the required third angle.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive the triangle's interior angles from three bearings, then use the sine rule to calculate two distances.

questions.mappingNote: Page 18 supplies the sine rule, page 19 demonstrates length calculations, and page 23 demonstrates a bearings sketch and angle setup. This question has a uniquely determined triangle; its requested quantities are sides.
questions.methodNote: Identify opposite side–angle pairs, derive interior angles from bearings, and rearrange the sine rule for lengths. Retain exact trigonometric expressions until the final rounding.
